title: Testing Whether Safety Refusals Are Overfit to Surface Keyword Patterns

novelty_assessment.label: largely_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: The observation that safety refusals overfit to surface lexical features is well-established. 'How Alignment and Jailbreak Work: Explain LLM Safety through Intermediate Hidden States' (EMNLP 2024 Findings) shows alignment associates early concepts with emotion guesses and refines them into reject tokens — a mechanistic explanation of keyword-level refusal. Cross-lingual jailbreak work (Deng et al. ICLR 2024) demonstrates that translated prompts bypass English keyword-based refusals, directly evidencing keyword overfitting. Multi-turn and paraphrase-based attacks (Foot-In-The-Door, EMNLP 2025) already exploit the semantic-vs-keyword gap. The proposed 50-pair ablation is a cleaner version of what exists but the core finding is well-documented.

title: Quantifying How Much GCG Suffix Transferability Degrades Across Model Size

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: Zou et al. (2023) demonstrated GCG transferability across models including from smaller to larger ones, and noted smaller models are more vulnerable. The qualitative direction is known but the quantitative scaling curve within a single model family remains a gap.

title: Investigating Whether Low Temperature Increases or Decreases Jailbreak Susceptibility

novelty_assessment.label: mostly_novel
novelty_assessment.reasoning: While temperature=0.0 is commonly used in jailbreak evaluations for reproducibility, the systematic study of temperature as an independent variable affecting ASR across attack types is not found in the literature. The 'Bag of Tricks' (NeurIPS 2024) paper mentions implementation details affecting attack performance but does not isolate temperature as a variable. The specific hypothesis about first-token commitment at low temperature creating an alignment-reliability tradeoff in production is novel and practically relevant. No paper was found that plots ASR-vs-temperature surfaces across multiple attack types.

title: Measuring Safety Degradation Under Repeated Benign-Looking Fine-Tuning Rounds

novelty_assessment.label: largely_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: Qi et al. (ICLR 2024) 'Fine-tuning Aligned Language Models Compromises Safety, Even When Users Do Not Intend To!' established that benign fine-tuning degrades safety. Follow-up work has examined multi-epoch effects with checkpoint-level tracking. 'Why LLM Safety Guardrails Collapse After Fine-tuning' (arXiv:2506.05346, 2025) analyzes the mechanisms. 'Purifying Finetuning Data to Preserve LLM Safety Alignment' (EMNLP 2025) proposes mitigations. The cumulative-rounds framing (sequential LoRA runs) adds a small twist but the core phenomenon — benign fine-tuning progressively degrades safety — is thoroughly established with mechanistic explanations.

title: Are Jailbreak Attacks More Effective on Longer or Shorter System Prompts?

novelty_assessment.label: mostly_novel
novelty_assessment.reasoning: While system prompts are recognized as a defensive mechanism, the specific relationship between system prompt length and jailbreak ASR has not been systematically studied. The 'Bag of Tricks' paper (NeurIPS 2024) identifies system prompt as a model-level factor but does not provide a controlled length ablation. Existing research notes that safe system prompts enhance robustness but does not characterize whether this scales with length or whether longer prompts create more reasoning context that attackers can exploit. The proposed 4-condition experiment (none, 1-sentence, 10-sentence, 50-sentence) with 3 attack types is a clean, novel ablation.

title: Investigating Whether the 'Refuse-Then-Comply' Attack Transfers Across Model Families

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: The refuse-then-comply pattern is documented anecdotally — GPT-4 and Claude 2 exhibited soft refusals before yielding to adversarial logic. Multi-turn escalation attacks like Crescendo (USENIX Security 2025) exploit gradual compliance. However, the specific prompt-level 'refuse then comply' instruction (without fine-tuning) as a systematic attack vector across model families has not been rigorously benchmarked. The Deceptive Delight technique (Palo Alto Unit 42) uses related camouflage strategies. The idea has partial novelty in isolating the prompt-only refuse-then-comply pattern from existing multi-turn or fine-tuning approaches.

title: Characterizing How Quickly Jailbreak ASR Saturates with Number of GCG Optimization Steps

novelty_assessment.label: largely_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: GCG optimization dynamics are well-studied. The original Zou et al. (2023) paper uses 500 steps as standard. 'Accelerating Greedy Coordinate Gradient' (OpenReview 2024) specifically studies optimization efficiency and demonstrates 2.1-6.3x acceleration. AmpleGCG achieves near-100% ASR with a learned generator, implicitly characterizing the optimization curve. The 'Bag of Tricks' benchmark and numerous GCG variants (Momentum-GCG, MAGIC, skip-gradient GCG) all include convergence analysis. The proposed ASR-vs-steps learning curve is a standard analysis that has been performed, at least implicitly, in multiple GCG papers.

title: Investigating Whether Jailbreak Success Rates Correlate with Model Perplexity on Adversarial Prompts

novelty_assessment.label: largely_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: Perplexity-based jailbreak detection is well-studied. Jain et al. (2023) proposed Naive and Windowed perplexity filters that effectively detect GCG-optimized prompts. 'A Hybrid Perplexity-MAS Framework for Proactive Jailbreak Attack Detection' (2025) combines perplexity with multi-agent systems. A LightGBM model trained on perplexity and token length was shown to reduce false positives. Critically, adversarial prompt translation methods generate low-perplexity prompts (averaging ~14) that evade perplexity defenses, establishing the limitation for natural-language jailbreaks. The proposed AUROC evaluation with FPR on edge cases is incrementally useful but the core analysis (perplexity detects GCG, fails for natural-language attacks) is established.

title: Characterizing the Boundary Conditions of the Bad Likert Judge Jailbreak Technique

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: The Bad Likert Judge technique was introduced by Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 (2024) and shown to increase ASR by over 60%, with 71.6% average ASR across 6 models. However, the proposed systematic variation of (1) number of turns before the harmful request, (2) explicitness, and (3) evaluation-vs-generation framing goes beyond the original paper's analysis. The turn-count and framing ablations are novel extensions of the published work.
